title: AI Saves Lives on Minefields

body_markdown:
***Ievgen Matiushenko** , Brussels*


*According to Ukrainian authorities and international partners, roughly 129,000 to 133,300 square kilometers of Ukraine’s territory remain potentially contaminated by landmines and explosive ordnance — more than 21% of the country’s area, or nearly a quarter of its territory. At the same time, more than 40,000 to 42,000 square kilometers of land have been returned to safe use since 2022–2023, along with around 5,000 square kilometers in 2026.*


*During the Ukraine Mine Action Conference in Brussels, international partners announced €70 million in funding for demining Ukrainian territories. In particular, the European Union announced €15 million in new financing to repair and maintain equipment for the State Emergency Service of Ukraine (SESU), survey and clear areas — primarily in the Kharkiv and Mykolaiv regions — and strengthen Ukrainian capacities. In addition, Switzerland committed 100 million Swiss francs for mine action in Ukraine through 2028, Japan announced grant aid of roughly 4 billion yen, Finland pledged an additional €2 million, and Norway announced €1.5 million through UNDP plus another €22 million planned for 2027.*


*​In a conversation with Ukrinform on the sidelines of the event in Brussels, co-founder and chief scientist of Safe Pro AI Dr. **Jasper Baur** spoke about how artificial intelligence and drones help detect explosive ordnance, what challenges Ukraine faces, and what hazards people encounter in fields and local communities.*


**ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IDENTIFIES MINE LOCATIONS BEFORE DEMINERS EVEN ENTER THE FIELD**


**​— Jasper, how and when did your company enter the Ukrainian market, and what technology underpins your work?**


​— We started doing research in landmine detection back in 2016 — before the full-scale invasion. At that time, we developed technology for detecting PFM-1 landmines in Afghanistan, because those are Soviet-era landmines. When the full-scale invasion happened in 2022, the technology we developed — which had been of limited use widely — became very useful because of the wide-scale contamination. So we decided we could help and apply this technology to detecting landmines on the surface and other unexploded ordnance (UXO).


​The technology essentially takes the power of drones, which can fly very large areas without having to put a person in danger stepping into a minefield. Before stepping into the minefield, you can fly a drone over and take many pictures. Then from those pictures you can analyze using an AI model trained on over 100,000 real-world images and other explosive ordnance. It systematically scans every image, finds where the landmines are, and geolocates them — basically putting them on a map. That allows deminers using the tool, before going into the field, to have a very good understanding of where the contamination is and which likely areas they have to prioritize for demining versus areas that likely have less contamination.


**​— Why is that approach important for deminers in practice, and does it require specialized hardware?**


​— It gives deminers a clear picture of the terrain before they step onto a hazardous site and helps lower risks to people. Our software is called SpotlightAI, and the company is Safe Pro AI (part of Safe Pro Group). It works with commercial off-the-shelf drones and does not require any special hardware — it can basically scale as long as you have a drone and a computer. Because of how it’s built, we’re aiming to grow it across mine action programs in Ukraine as well as in the 58 other countries around the world that are contaminated with landmines and UXO.


**— How much does this speed up the work, and which Ukrainian bodies are already using your technology?**


​— It’s more efficient, safer, and faster. According to a study by Norwegian People’s Aid, using the technology resulted in 4.4 times more detections compared to the traditional method of using drones without AI searching through the imagery.


​In Ukraine, we partner with the State Special Transport Service (SSTS), the State Emergency Service of Ukraine (SESU), and international demining organizations like Norwegian People’s Aid. We have also signed a memorandum of understanding with Kyiv Polytechnic Institute (KPI) and the Educational and Scientific Center for Innovations in Humanitarian Demining at KPI — mostly around educational and training programs, including for SESU, as well as evaluating the use of the technology in Ukraine. Our SpotlightAI product also won in the scalable innovation category at the Mine Action Innovation Award run by the Geneva International Centre for Humanitarian Demining (GICHD) with EU support, and in Ukraine we have recorded around 60,000 confirmed detections.


**WE HAVE SURVEYED AND MAPPED ABOUT 16,000 HECTARES OF LAND**


**​— How do your outputs connect with demining operators and explosive ordnance risk education?**


​— There is a clear distinction in roles. What we produce does not directly handle explosive ordnance risk education (EORE), though demining organizations can use our information. For instance, once a PFM-1 is detected in a field, that information can be broadcast to the community to raise awareness and make sure information from detection is passed along. Meanwhile, demining operators are the ones doing the clearance work on the ground.


**​— You mentioned contaminated farmland. How acute is this problem for Ukraine?**


​— It is a major problem for the agricultural sector. We’ve surveyed around 16,000 hectares of land and mapped it out, and the majority of that is in Mykolaiv, which is agricultural fields. So most of the mines we have detected are in agricultural fields.


​Farmers themselves aren’t usually doing the surveying or demining because it’s very dangerous, although in some cases they do, often under pressure for economic reasons. The better thing is for them to call the right authorities, such as the State Emergency Service, and put in a report so authorized teams go in and do the clearance. There are also state support mechanisms that help fund demining on farmland, but farmers themselves shouldn’t be in charge of doing the clearance.


**​— Can your system detect mines underground or underwater, and how does it adapt to changing Russian tactics?**


​— It focuses on objects on the surface. We do find subsurface indicators — such as crater holes or things that might indicate an object is buried — but we’re not doing direct subsurface detection. As for waterways, we haven’t done direct underwater detection, though floods — such as after the 2023 Kakhovka dam break — moved mines over long distances and affected surface conditions. Chemical detection generally requires ground-based sensors rather than drones.


​At the same time, the war is dynamic, and we constantly have to update our models to keep up with the realities of the battlefield. New ordnance and improvised explosive devices are dropped, and Russian forces modify munitions and use 3D printing. Recently, we’ve seen sticks that have been modified with explosives inside and dropped from drones. To a farmer or driver, a stick or branch in a field or along a road looks ordinary, but stepping on it or driving over it can cause an explosion. There are also booby traps — for instance, an anti-personnel pressure mine placed beneath an anti-tank mine — as well as 3D-printed mine casings disguised with moss or branches, which complicates both detection and risk education.


**​— Do local residents — in forests or fields — still get hurt because risks aren’t obvious or aren’t fully understood?**


​— When munitions are 3D-printed or camouflaged to look like a tree branch or moss, it makes explaining the risks to communities much harder. That is why it is critical that people don’t touch suspicious items and report them to authorities, while our models keep adapting to what appears on the ground.


**AS LONG AS HOSTILITIES CONTINUE AND NEW MINES ARE BEING LAID, COMPLETING DEMINING OPERATIONS IS EXTREMELY DIFFICULT**


**​— What are the biggest challenges you see for humanitarian demining in Ukraine over the coming years?**


​— Initially, the biggest challenges were technical: building a database, making sure the models work well, and quantifying how they work in different environments. Technically, we have overcome that and have a very solid solution.


​Now, two main factors stand out. First is economics and sustainable funding: demining is not cheap, and it’s important that funding is sustainable for both the organizations doing innovation and the ones doing demining. Second is legal frameworks and standards: legislation and standards need to catch up to drones and AI in the modern era so new innovations are recognized by the demining community as new methods.


**​— How strongly do security conditions and the course of the war affect the pace of demining?**


​— That is a huge factor. Because of increased threats — including Shahed drones and FPV drones targeting humanitarian demining operations — the buffer zone for humanitarian demining from the front line had to be expanded from 20 kilometers to 50 kilometers. When demining partners are hit and have to pause operations or run at reduced capacity, it directly affects data processing and overall progress. As long as fighting continues and new mines are laid, completing demining is very difficult, so much depends on when the war ends and how steady the funding and support remain.
